title: Boethius in prison
hookLine: awaiting execution around 524, Boethius writes The Consolation of Philosophy, where Philosophy visits him as a woman (Consolation 1)

lines: FROM HIGH OFFICE TO A CELL.
SAD POEMS IN A DARK HOUR.
cards: A man who had everything is sitting in a cell. Not long ago he held high office in Italy. His two sons were made consuls on the same day, and he gave the speech.
Now he's been accused of treason, condemned without a real hearing, and he's waiting to be killed. He does the natural thing in a dark hour: he writes sad poems about how unfair it all is.
And then, in his book, someone walks into the cell.

teach.b: Boethius was a Roman senator serving Theodoric, the Gothic king who ruled Italy, and a scholar steeped in Greek philosophy.
In the book he says he was accused of treason partly for defending another senator, and condemned far away, without being heard. He was executed not long after. Second, the visitor.

The Consolation of Philosophy opens with Boethius weeping over verses, the Muses of poetry gathered round him. Then a woman appears, hard to measure: sometimes ordinary height, sometimes her head seems to touch the sky.

teach.h: HER ROBE TORN BY RIVAL SCHOOLS.
teach.b: Her robe is woven with Greek letters and a ladder between them, and it's torn. She's Philosophy. She sends the Muses away, and sits down on his bed.
Third, the torn robe. She explains it: after Socrates and Plato, rival crowds tried to seize her, Epicureans and Stoics among them, each tearing away a scrap and thinking they had the whole.
It's a fitting image after this week of neighbors. Fourth, what kind of book it is.
Boethius was a Christian; he wrote works of theology.

Yet the Consolation never names Christ and argues from philosophy alone. Scholars still debate why. He talks with Philosophy, in prose and poetry, about fortune, happiness and God, while waiting to die.
And it begins with something anyone can do in a hard hour: stop only lamenting, and let a wiser voice, even your own, ask you some questions.

how: Readers have turned to Boethius's Consolation of Philosophy in times of loss and injustice, some reading it as a dialogue with their own wiser mind.

games.q: you're Boethius, condemned, writing sad verses with the Muses of poetry. Philosophy walks in. what does she do first?
o: sends the Muses away and sits down on your bed.
games.why: she drives off the Muses who were feeding his grief, sits beside him, and begins to ask him questions.

practice: Think of something hard in your life right now, or recently, and let yourself feel the complaint. Then imagine a calm, wise presence sitting down beside you: Philosophy, or a grandparent, or the best version of yourself.
What's the first question they'd ask, not advice but a question? If you have something to write with, jot it down and begin an answer.

wordCard.voice: Theodoric. The Gothic king Boethius served as a Roman senator before being condemned and imprisoned, awaiting execution. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: consolation, comfort. Consolatio Philosophiae, the comfort that philosophy gives.

carryVoice: Your line: philosophy visits. Even in a cell, a wiser voice can ask a question. Another week of neighbors, complete.
